questions.text: Which of the following is the most appropriate title for the passage?
questions.context: When a disease outbreak is first detected, public health officials often assume the earliest reported case counts already capture the outbreak's true scale, an assumption that shapes how quickly a response is scaled. Retrospective analysis of past outbreaks complicates this assumption considerably: mild or entirely asymptomatic cases routinely go undetected in an outbreak's earliest weeks, meaning the true number of infections at any given moment is almost always substantially higher than official counts suggest, sometimes by a factor of ten or more. Officials who wait for confirmed case counts to justify a response therefore risk acting weeks after the outbreak's actual scale would have warranted a far earlier intervention.

options.text: Why Official Case Counts Always Overstate an Outbreak's True Scale
Why Early Outbreak Case Counts Systematically Understate the True Number of Infections
A History of Disease Surveillance Methods
Why Public Health Officials Always Respond Too Quickly
How Asymptomatic Cases Are Diagnosed in Clinical Settings

questions.text: Choose the most appropriate topic of the passage.
questions.context: A museum that reports rising annual visitor enrollment in its membership programme is often assumed to be attracting a genuinely broader, more contemporary audience than in previous decades. Attendance data broken down by age and repeat-visit frequency complicates this assumption: much of the reported growth turns out to come from existing members renewing rather than new members joining, meaning the museum's actual audience base may be barely expanding at all even as headline membership numbers climb steadily year after year, since a stable core of repeat visitors renewing consistently produces exactly the same growth curve as genuine audience expansion would.

options.text: the historical development of museum membership programmes
how rising membership numbers can mask a stagnant audience base rather than genuine audience expansion
the total revenue museums generate from membership fees annually
why museums rarely publish detailed membership renewal data
a comparison of two specific museums' membership growth rates

questions.text: Choose the most appropriate topic of the passage.
questions.context: A defendant's decision to concentrate legal resources on discrediting a single key witness, rather than spreading limited resources across contesting every piece of evidence, is often assumed by observers to reflect a weak overall case. Trial strategists who study jury deliberations closely find the opposite pattern just as often true: juries asked to weigh dozens of contested details frequently lose track of which pieces actually mattered, while a defence that concentrates entirely on one witness's credibility gives jurors a single, memorable thread to follow through an otherwise complicated case, sometimes producing an acquittal precisely because the strategy appeared, superficially, too narrow to be a genuine defence.

options.text: the legal qualifications required to become a defence attorney
how concentrating a defence on a single witness's credibility can be a deliberately effective strategy, not a sign of weakness
the total number of jury trials held annually in a given country
why juries are instructed to disregard a defendant's demeanour
a comparison of two specific historical jury trials

questions.text: Which of the following best states the main point of the passage?
questions.context: Species that reproduce in enormous numbers, producing thousands of offspring per breeding cycle, are sometimes assumed to be evolutionarily more successful than species that reproduce sparingly, since a larger raw number of offspring intuitively seems safer against extinction. Population biologists studying long-term survival rates complicate this assumption: species investing heavily in a small number of offspring, providing extensive parental care to each, often show more stable population trends over centuries than species relying on sheer reproductive volume, since quality of individual survival, not raw quantity produced, ultimately determines a population's long-term stability.

options.text: Species producing the most offspring are always the most evolutionarily successful.
Long-term population stability may depend more on offspring survival quality than on raw reproductive volume.
Species with extensive parental care always produce more offspring overall.
Population biologists agree that reproductive strategy has no effect on long-term survival.
Extinction risk is entirely unrelated to a species' reproductive strategy.

questions.text: How many of the statements below do NOT agree with the passage?
questions.context:
I spent the first year after my divorce assuming my friendships would naturally sort themselves out, that the people who mattered would simply come over more often once I was living alone, and the rest would quietly fade without any effort on my part. What actually happened was closer to the opposite: the friends I heard from most were the ones I had, without quite realising it, been the one reaching out to all along, and several people I had assumed were close friends never once initiated contact once I stopped doing it for both of us. A friend I hadn't spoken to in years reunited with me entirely by accident at a mutual acquaintance's birthday, and we have been close ever since, closer than several people I had actively maintained contact with throughout the marriage.

Statements
(a) The writer initially assumed friendships would sort themselves out naturally after the divorce.
(b) The friends who stayed in contact were, in most cases, the ones the writer had been reaching out to.
(c) Every person the writer assumed was a close friend continued initiating contact afterward.
(d) The writer reunited with an old friend by accident at a mutual acquaintance's birthday.
(e) The writer became closer with this reunited friend than with some people maintained throughout the marriage.
(f) The writer deliberately arranged the reunion with the old friend in advance.

questions.text: Which statement does NOT agree with the two explanations given in the passage?
questions.context: Contemporary artworks by a living artist sometimes sell at auction for prices far exceeding anything the same artist commanded just years earlier, a jump two competing explanations attempt to account for. One explanation holds that a single prominent collector's public purchase confers a kind of institutional legitimacy on the artist, after which other collectors, previously uncertain how to value largely untested contemporary work, treat that purchase as reliable confirmation of genuine long-term value. A second, competing explanation instead proposes that auction prices for contemporary art are driven substantially by scarcity manufactured through the artist's own limited output, meaning the price jump reflects collectors competing over an increasingly limited supply of new pieces rather than any change in perceived artistic merit at all.

options.text: The first explanation attributes the price jump to institutional legitimacy conferred by a prominent collector's purchase.
The first explanation suggests other collectors treat that purchase as confirmation of genuine long-term value.
The second explanation claims the artist's output has become more abundant rather than more limited.
The second explanation attributes the price jump to competition over an increasingly scarce supply of new pieces.
Both explanations attempt to account for the same sharp rise in a living artist's auction prices.

questions.context: Coastal fortifications built to withstand naval bombardment relied heavily on angled, sloped walls rather than the vertical walls typical of earlier inland fortresses, since a sloped surface deflects a cannonball's impact rather than absorbing its full force directly. Military engineers who studied the effectiveness of these coastal forts found that sloped-wall designs suffered measurably less structural damage per assault than vertical-wall designs facing an identical bombardment, a finding that led most coastal powers to adopt sloped fortification as standard practice within a few decades, even as the underlying cannon technology itself continued to improve independently of any change in fortification design.
